# How to Train a Dog: A Kid’s Guide to Being a Great Dog Trainer

Training a dog can be one of the most fun things to do with your pet! Dogs are amazing animals, and they learn best when training feels like a game. Kids can help train a dog too, but it is important to be gentle, patient, and safe.

Here are some easy steps to help you train your dog like a pro.

## 1. Start With a Happy Dog

Dogs learn better when they feel calm and happy. Before you start training, let your dog sniff around or play for a little while. A relaxed dog is more ready to learn.

## 2. Use Treats and Praise

Dogs love treats! When your dog does something good, give them a tiny treat, a pet, or a happy “Good dog!” Right away.

You do not need a lot of treats. A few tiny pieces are enough. Remember: less is often better, especially if your dog needs to stay healthy.

## 3. Teach One Simple Trick at a Time

Start with an easy trick like “sit.” Here is how to do it:

1. Hold a treat near your dog’s nose.
2. Slowly move the treat up and back over their head.
3. When your dog’s bottom touches the ground, say “Sit!”
4. Give them the treat and praise.

Practice for just a few minutes at a time. Dogs learn best with short, fun sessions.

## 4. Be Patient

Sometimes dogs need time to understand what you want. If your dog does not get it right away, do not get frustrated. Take a break and try again later. Training should feel like play, not stress.

## 5. Practice Every Day

A little practice each day can make a big difference. You can practice during breakfast, after school, or before bedtime. The more you practice, the more your dog will remember.

## 6. Make Training a Game

Dogs love games! You can hide treats around the room and teach your dog to “find” them. You can also practice tricks before going outside for a walk. This makes training feel like part of the fun.

## 7. End With a Finale

At the end of each training session, finish with a trick your dog already knows well. This is the finale! It makes your dog feel successful, and you both end the session feeling happy.

## A Kid’s Final Tip

Always ask a grown-up before training a dog, especially if the dog is new or shy. Never pull on a dog’s ears or tail, and never train when the dog looks scared or tired.

With kindness, practice, and a little patience, you can help your dog learn cool tricks and become the best dog ever!

A lonely Hue sits on a shelf,  
half-faded, quiet, still.  
Not red enough to shout,  
not blue enough to chill.  

*My name is Hue, and I feel like a color no one chooses.*  

I play singles late at night,  
tiny songs that know my ache;  
they pass through headphones, soft and brief,  
then fade for my own sake.  

At school the hallway buzzes,  
but I’m a shade apart.  
I hum the same old singles,  
hoping someone maps my heart.  

Maybe one day the light will find me,  
turn me bright and true—  
until then I’m just a lonely Hue,  
waiting, still, and new.

The U.S. maternity leave policy is pretty mixed, because there is no single federal law that guarantees paid maternity leave. The main federal law is the Family and Medical Leave Act. FMLA can give eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for pregnancy, childbirth, or newborn care. That leave is job-protected, which means the employer generally has to hold the job or an equivalent one for the worker. But FMLA does not require the employer to pay the employee during that leave. So many people use vacation days, sick days, or other paid time off if they have it. Some employers also offer paid parental leave as a company benefit, but that is not required by federal law. FMLA eligibility can be strict, since the worker usually needs to have worked for the employer for at least 12 months. The employee also usually needs 1,250 hours of work in the past 12 months. The employer also needs to be covered, which often means it has 50 or more employees in a certain area. That means many small-business workers may not qualify for FMLA even if they need leave. Pregnant employees may also have protections under the Americans with Disabilities Act if pregnancy causes a disability or if they need reasonable accommodations. The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act can also require reasonable workplace accommodations in many cases. So the U.S. system is basically a patchwork of federal law, state law, and employer policy.

Section 2

State laws can matter a lot because some states have paid family leave programs. These programs may provide partial wage replacement for new parents, but the rules vary by state. In some states, employers must offer paid sick leave, and that leave can sometimes be used for pregnancy recovery. Some states also have their own family leave laws that cover smaller employers or lower eligibility thresholds. # The Benefits of Using a Digital Marketing Agency

Digital marketing agencies bring specialized expertise that many businesses struggle to develop internally.  
They understand search engines, social platforms, paid advertising, email marketing, and analytics tools in depth.  
This expertise helps companies avoid common mistakes that waste time and budget.  
An experienced agency can also create a cohesive marketing strategy instead of scattered tactics.  
Businesses often benefit from an agency because it provides access to tools that may be too expensive to purchase alone.  
Agencies also stay current with algorithm changes, platform updates, and emerging trends.  
This allows brands to remain competitive in a fast-changing online environment.  
One major benefit is improved efficiency, since agencies can manage campaigns more quickly than in-house teams.  
They can also scale efforts up or down based on seasonal demand or business goals.  
Another advantage is an outside perspective, which can reveal blind spots in messaging or positioning.  
Agencies often bring data-driven thinking, helping businesses make decisions based on performance rather than assumptions.  
With access to analytics, agencies can track traffic, conversions, customer behavior, and return on investment.  
This reporting helps companies understand which channels are working and which need adjustment.  
A digital marketing agency can also improve brand consistency across websites, ads, and social media.  
Consistent branding builds trust and makes a business more memorable to potential customers.  
Agencies are skilled at creating content that resonates with target audiences and drives action.  
They can design landing pages, manage email campaigns, and optimize ads for better results.  
Using an agency can also free internal teams to focus on core business activities.  
Instead of learning every new platform, business owners can spend time on products, services, and customers.  
Agencies often provide faster access to creative resources, such as designers, copywriters, and video editors.  
This reduces delays and helps companies maintain a steady marketing presence.  
In many cases, hiring an agency is more cost-effective than building a full marketing department from scratch.  
A strong agency partnership can therefore increase visibility, generate leads, and support long-term growth.

Good morning, students. Today we are going to look at what is inside Shinto shrines, using a shrine such as [shrine name] at [address] as our example.

*The inner sanctuary and the hidden sacred presence*  
Inside a Shinto shrine, the most important space is usually the honden, or main sanctuary. This is where the kami, the sacred presence, is believed to reside. Inside the honden may be a goshintai, or sacred object. This could be a mirror, a sword, a jewel, a scroll, a stone, a tree branch, or another object that represents the kami. Often, the goshintai is not visible to visitors. For example, on [date], a visitor might see the shrine buildings but not the sacred object itself.

*The worship hall and ritual space*  
In front of the honden is often the haiden, or worship hall. This is where people pray, make offerings, and participate in rituals. Inside this area, you may find offering tables, bells, ropes, paper streamers, and sometimes a place for kagura, which is sacred music and dance. The space is designed to help people approach the kami with respect.

*Offerings, symbols, and shrine treasures*  
Many shrines also contain smaller storage rooms or treasure halls. Inside these may be ritual tools, sacred robes, musical instruments, historical documents, and gifts from worshippers. Common symbolic objects include shimenawa, which are sacred ropes, and shide, which are white paper streamers. You may also see ema, small wooden tablets for wishes, and omikuji, paper fortunes. These items show that a shrine is not only a religious building but also a living center of community memory and devotion.

*Voice so smooth it could sell ice to a penguin town.*

A poem should be a teapot,

photosynthesize

Let me tell you about the reductions—  
not math reductions, but church reductions,  
those mission towns the Jesuits built  
in the forests and grasslands around the Paraná and Uruguay rivers,  
mostly in the 1600s and 1700s.

They were called “reductions”  
because they reduced scattered Guaraní villages  
into one planned town:  
a church square, a bell, a school,  
a workshop, a hospital,  
fields divided by family,  
and a calendar of saints’ days  
that replaced the old feast days  
with new saints in red vestments.

You could hear the bells before you saw the church:  
San Ignacio Miní, Santa Ana, Loreto,  
the Jesuit fathers teaching catechism in Guaraní,  
carving saints with the same hands  
that later carved altars,  
while the church taught them to write, sing,  
and sometimes fight for their homes.

It was not a simple story.  
Some called it protection;  
some called it a cage.  
The Guaraní worked the land,  
paid no tribute to the crown,  
kept their language,  
but also learned to fear the whip,  
the priest, the plague, the soldier,  
and the map-makers in Europe  
who moved borders like moving furniture.

Then came the Treaty of Madrid,  
1750, the Portuguese crown trading  
one mission town for another,  
and the Guaraní said: no.  
The Jesuits, awkward as ever,  
were caught between obedience and conscience,  
and in the end the church’s experiment  
was crushed by empires that preferred silence.

Today the stone ruins are quiet,  
but in Misiones, Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil,  
people still talk about them—  
some as heritage, some as grief,  
some as a fiesta where saints dance  
with drums that remember

Mira loved the little clamshell glowing on her lap, its blue night screen a door she could not leave again.
Every morning she woke and reached beneath her pillow for the soft plastic moon that hummed with secret worlds waiting.
She carried it through breakfast, through school, through rain, because the tiny kingdom inside needed her before the day began.
Her name was not just Mira to the pixels; it was the hero who could mend the broken moon.
She tapped, she slid, she blew softly on the microphone as if breath could wake sleeping dragons.
In class, she drew maps of invisible towns while chalk dust fell like snow on a forgotten battlefield.
At recess, she sat apart, eyes lowered, smiling at a quest only she could see unfold.
The DS spoke to her in bright beeps and gentle chimes, a language softer than the noisy hall.
Her friends called it strange, but she did not mind; they had no portal in their pockets.
At night, she lay awake, and the DS glowed like a lantern in the dark, a small brave star.
She caught fish, she cooked cakes, she saved dragons from cages made of code and careful dreams.
She fed a dog made of light and learned its name by heart, though it would never wag.
Her mother took the game away and said, “Look up; the real world is waiting for you now.”
Mira stared at walls, and the silence was a level she did not know how to clear.
Without the DS, colors seemed too loud, and hours moved like slow water under ice.
She missed the hush of plastic, the snap of cases, the way a saved game kept her safe.
Then one rainy afternoon, she opened a blank notebook and began to draw the creatures she had loved.
She drew the moon dog, the crystal fish, the tiny knight who rode a paper bird.
She drew doors and keys and stars, and the pages filled like worlds escaping from her mind.
Her mother asked, “Where did these come from?” and Mira whispered, “They came through the small blue door.”
She learned that a screen is a window, not a whole house, and windows are made to open.
Still, when night came, she unlocked the DS once more, but gently, as one greets an old friend.
She played for a little while, then closed it, and the quiet room became a kingdom too.

Once upon a time, in a kingdom of very dramatic doorknobs and suspiciously cheerful handshakes, a bard stood at the village square and declared, “I know a riddle so tricky it made a wizard sneeze twice.”

The villagers gathered, mostly because the wizard’s hat had fallen into the soup.

“What can you catch but not throw?” asked the bard, holding up a single tissue like it was a sacred sword.

The blacksmith shouted, “A ball!”

“No,” said the bard.

The farmer yelled, “A fish!”

“Also no,” the bard replied. “A fish can be thrown, usually when someone is trying to prove they’ve had too much ale.”

Then the bard grinned and announced the answer: “A cold!”

The crowd gasped. One child said, “But I threw one at my brother.”

“You sneezed on him,” the bard corrected. “That is not throwing. That is biological betrayal.”

Thus began the tale of Barnaby the Unlucky, a man who caught a cold from *the sneeze that launched a thousand tissues*. He tried to get rid of it by throwing it at a duck, but the duck simply looked offended and waddled away. He tried to throw it at a tree, and the tree dropped a branch on his head. He even tried to throw it at his rival, only to accidentally throw a sock instead.

By the end, Barnaby learned the moral: *the legendary ball that could not be hurled*. Some things in life you can catch, but if you try to throw them, you end up looking like a confused statue holding a used tissue.

This airborne moment is one of the most dramatic points in gymnastics because it reveals both preparation and risk. The gymnast’s speed, balance, and spatial awareness must all be precise, since gravity will eventually reclaim the body.

The phrase *performing a stunt* broadens the scene beyond a simple jump. A stunt implies difficulty, intention, and skill. It may be a flip, twist, leap, or combination of rotations, each requiring confidence and training. The word stunt can also carry a sense of spectacle, as though the movement is meant to be admired, challenged, or tested. The gymnast is not merely moving; the gymnast is executing something deliberate, something that demands coordination between mind and muscle. In this way, the sentence suggests a moment of mastery, but also a moment of vulnerability, because the body is exposed to the laws of physics.

The setting implied by the sentence is equally important. *In the air* creates a temporary space where the gymnast seems to hover, defying ordinary expectations of movement. It invites the viewer to imagine the surrounding environment: a gymnasium, a competition hall, a crowd holding its breath, or a quiet practice room. The background may be blurred by motion, while the gymnast’s form remains the focal point. The sentence also implies sound, tension, and anticipation, even if none is explicitly described.

Finally, the statement highlights *physical control*, *risk*, *artistry*, and *momentum*. Each of these elements helps explain why the sentence feels dynamic. The gymnast’s airborne body becomes both subject and symbol: a person testing limits while maintaining discipline.

## Rubric for Rating a Teenager’s Essay

| Category | Excellent (4) | Proficient (3) | Developing (2) | Needs Improvement (1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Thesis / Main Idea** | Clear, focused, and specific claim that guides the essay. | Clear main idea, but may be general or partially developed. | Main idea is present but unclear or inconsistent. | No clear main idea, or the essay lacks focus. |
| **Organization** | Logical structure with strong introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. | Generally organized with a recognizable structure. | Some organization, but ideas may be repetitive or unclear. | Disorganized or difficult to follow. |
| **Support / Evidence** | Strong, relevant examples, details, or explanations support the main idea. | Adequate support, though some points may need more development. | Limited or weak evidence; some claims are unsupported. | Little or no relevant support. |
| **Analysis / Thinking** | Shows insight, originality, and clear reasoning. | Shows some thoughtfulness and explanation. | Mostly summarizes or describes with limited analysis. | Ideas are shallow, vague, or off-topic. |
| **Language & Style** | Clear, varied, and appropriate language for the audience and purpose. | Mostly clear writing with some variety and control. | Awkward or unclear phrasing in places. | Frequent language problems that interfere with meaning. |
| **Grammar & Mechanics** | Few or no errors in grammar, punctuation, spelling, or sentence structure. | Minor errors that do not greatly affect meaning. | Several errors that sometimes distract from meaning. | Many errors that make the essay hard to understand. |

### Suggested Scoring
- **24–30:** Excellent  
- **18–23:** Good  
- **12–17:** Developing  
- **6–11:** Needs Improvement  

******

"the most common signs and symptoms of abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer often develop gradually and may be mistaken for benign gynecologic, urinary, or gastrointestinal problems. because ovarian cancer can spread along peritoneal surfaces and within the pelvis, symptoms frequently reflect irritation, mass effect, obstruction, fluid accumulation, and systemic illness. one of the most typical presentations is progressive abdominal distension or bloating that does not resolve with diet, laxatives, or antacids. patients may describe a feeling of fullness, tightness, or heaviness in the abdomen that worsens over weeks or months. early satiety is another important symptom, meaning that the person feels full after eating only a small amount of food. this may occur because ascites, tumor bulk, or involvement of the stomach and upper abdomen reduces space for food or affects normal gastric filling.

pelvic pain or pressure is also common when disease involves the ovaries, uterus, broad ligaments, bladder, rectum, or peritoneal surfaces. the pain may be dull, constant, or worsened by intercourse, bowel movements, urination, or prolonged standing. some patients notice a sense of pelvic heaviness, a mass, or discomfort that feels different from usual menstrual cramps. abdominal pain may be diffuse if there is widespread peritoneal irritation or localized if a large pelvic mass, ovarian cyst rupture, torsion, or bowel involvement is present.

ascites, which is accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, is a frequent sign of advanced ovarian cancer and abdominal spread. it can cause rapid abdominal enlargement, tight clothing, shortness of breath, poor appetite, and a sensation of fluid shifting when moving. ascites may also lead to discomfort, reflux, and difficulty sleeping. in some cases, pleural effusion can occur, causing shortness of breath, cough, or reduced exercise tolerance, especially when disease has spread beyond the pelvis.

gastrointestinal symptoms are common because peritoneal dissemination can affect the bowel, omentum, and mesentery. patients may experience nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, excessive gas, or a feeling of incomplete bowel evacuation. bowel obstruction is an important complication of abdominal spread and may present with vomiting, inability to pass stool or gas, abdominal tenderness, and progressive distension. omental disease, sometimes described as a thickened or nodular omentum, can contribute to a palpable upper abdominal mass and increased abdominal girth.

I woke up in a bottega, turpentine and chalk,  
A Medici in my earpiece, telling me to walk  
Into vanishing-point streets, marble, moon, and talk,  
Where a anatomist sketches angels in the hawk.  

Gold leaf on my eyelids, ultramarine in my cup,  
I’m painting saints with real dirt, making heaven look up.  
Florence got a fever dream, cathedral on my chest,  
Da Vinci in the mirror saying, “Put the nerve to test.”  

I’m blending shadows, sfumato, smoke in the mouth,  
A humanist with a compass, mapping truth to south.  
No flat icons, no stiff crowns, no paper-thin gods—  
I made the Madonna breathe, I made the marble nod.

> **Renaissance, not a costume party, it’s a lens!**

> **We turned the whole world sideways with geometrical signs!**

> **We put the human face in outer space!**

A Florentine ghost wearing a powdered shirt.

A small gray cat named Momo lived in a house by the sea.
His family loved him with warm hands and soft voices.
Every morning, *the sun* spilled across his sleeping mat.
He chased paper balls and purred under the kitchen table.
His favorite boy, Leo, always saved a piece of fish for him.
Momo believed his world was safe and endless.
One winter evening, a strange wind rattled the windows.
The house filled with flashing lights and urgent voices.
Momo hid beneath the bed and trembled.
When he finally crept out, the rooms were empty.
*The door* stood open to a dark lane.
He waited for footsteps that never came.
He sniffed the floor for their familiar scents.
The smell of fish had gone cold.
Momo meowed until his throat felt dry.
No one answered.
Hunger pushed him into the street.
*The rain* began to fall in silver needles.
He ran past closed shops and wet cobblestones.
A dog barked, and Momo fled into an alley.
He slept behind a crate shivering.
The next day, he found a bakery with a cracked door.
A baker dropped a crust, and Momo ate it quickly.
For three days, he returned to the same alley.
The baker left a saucer of milk outside.
Momo drank it and blinked slowly.
Still, he searched the neighborhood for his family.
*Every house* looked like the one he had left.
He climbed fences and peeked through windows.
He listened for Leo's whistle at dusk.
One night, a car stopped near the bakery.
A woman stepped out and called a name.
Momo heard it and froze.
It was not his family, but it sounded close.
He followed the woman through *a narrow gate*.
She had a basket full of old blankets.
She saw him and sat down gently.
"Hello, little one," she said softly.
Momo did not run.
She offered him a scrap of chicken.
He ate it and leaned against her shoe.
Her name was Mara, and she had lost a cat years before.
She carried him home in *a wool scarf*.
His new bed was small but warm.
Momo still looked toward the sea at night.
Sometimes he dreamed of Leo's voice

They do not require much planning. A person who lives near a green space may visit it every day, and if that person owns a dog, the dog becomes part of the routine. # How to Conduct a Job Interview

Conducting a job interview is one of the most important steps in hiring the right person for a role. A well-structured interview helps employers evaluate candidates fairly, understand their skills and experience, and assess whether they will fit within the company culture. Whether you are interviewing for a technical role, a customer service position, or a leadership job, preparation and consistency are key.

## 1. Prepare Before the Interview

Before meeting with a candidate, review the job description and identify the key qualifications you are looking for. These may include technical skills, communication abilities, problem-solving skills, or leadership experience.

It is also helpful to prepare a list of interview questions in advance. For example, you might ask: **[question]**

Preparation ensures that the interview remains focused and that each candidate is evaluated using similar criteria.

## 2. Create a Welcoming Environment

A good interview begins by making the candidate feel comfortable. Start by greeting them politely, introducing yourself, and explaining the purpose of the interview. You should also let the candidate know how long the interview will last and what they can expect during the process.

A comfortable candidate is more likely to communicate clearly and present their true abilities.

## 3. Ask Relevant Questions

Use a mix of behavioral, situational, and technical questions to understand how the candidate thinks and performs. Behavioral questions help you learn about past experiences, while situational questions reveal how they might handle future challenges.

For example, you can ask: “Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline.” This type of question helps you understand the candidate’s work habits, stress management, and problem-solving skills.

## 4. Listen Carefully

During the interview, listen more than you speak. Pay attention to the candidate’s answers, tone, and examples. Strong candidates often provide specific stories that demonstrate their skills and achievements.

Avoid interrupting too often, and take brief notes if allowed. This helps you remember important details when making your decision.

## 5. Evaluate Consistently

To reduce bias, compare all candidates using the same evaluation standards. Consider factors such as experience, communication, cultural fit, and overall potential. It can help to score each candidate on key competencies rather than relying only on first impressions.

## 6. Close the Interview Professionally

At the end of the interview, give the candidate a chance to ask questions. This shows respect for their interest in the role. Explain the next steps in the hiring process and provide a realistic timeline for making a decision.

A professional closing leaves a positive impression of your company, even if the candidate is not selected.

## Conclusion

A successful job interview requires preparation, clear communication, and fair evaluation. By planning ahead, asking meaningful questions, and listening carefully, you can identify candidates who are not only qualified but also well-suited for your organization.

Poem 1

There is a morning ritual, bright as a kitchen window,
when I lift the foil and see my hair catch fire.
Not the old brown, not the quiet brown that listened too long,
but copper, plum, seafoam, a color that says hello
before I even speak.

Joy arrives in strands.
It rinses through the sink like a small rainbow learning to swim.
It stains the shampoo bottle, the towel, my fingertips,
and I become a painter who never needed permission,
a cartographer of impossible maps.

At the bus stop, strangers smile as if I brought them candy.
At the mirror, I am someone who dared to ask,
“What if the crown of my head could be a garden,
could be a comet, could be a warning label,
could be a question mark with curls?”

Dyed hair is a secret kept in public,
a small rebellion that needs no shouting.
It turns the ordinary comb into a wand,
the wind into a curtain,
the day into a chance to shine.

******

Poem 2

I woke up violet, and the world woke up with me.
Sunlight poured through the blinds and caught the tips,
making my hair a field of tiny lanterns,
a parade I could wear without a drum.

People said, “That color suits you,”
and the sentence bounced along my spine like laughter.
I walked taller, not because I was taller,
but because the color had given me a new gravity,
a way of floating while still touching the ground.

There is joy in the rinse,
in the blue-green water spiraling down the drain,
in the smell of the treatment,
in the way the strands feel softer, stranger,
as if each one became a note in a song.

Rain makes it darker, deeper,
as though my hair is holding a bruised plum sky.
Night makes it glow,
as though I walked out of a painting
where the artist used a brush made of joy.

I do not dye my hair to hide.
I dye it to announce:
I am here, I am changing, I am bright,
and every new shade is a door
I can open without knocking.

I am a dwelling with no foundation, no roof of tiles, no chimney, no windows, and no doors that open onto a yard. I am not made of wood, stone, brick, glass, or metal, though I may imitate their forms with astonishing grace. I stand because of balance, not because of strength. I fall because of air, not because of age. A sneeze can unmake me. A footstep can betray me. A child’s laugh can scatter my walls. A table tremble can bring my towers down.

I am often born in silence, when someone sits quietly and dares the world to stay still. Unity and Difference: Understanding the Distinctions Between Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims

When people speak of Islam, they often imagine a single, unified religious community. In reality, Islam is a vast and diverse civilization with many traditions, legal schools, theological movements, and cultural expressions. Among these traditions, the two largest branches are Sunni and Shi‘a Islam. Both communities share the foundational beliefs of Islam: belief in one God, acceptance of Muhammad as the final prophet, reverence for the Qur’an, and commitment to prayer, fasting, charity, pilgrimage, and ethical conduct. Nevertheless, the distinction between Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims has shaped Islamic history, law, spirituality, and politics for more than fourteen centuries. Understanding these differences requires more than a simple comparison of beliefs. It requires attention to history, authority, religious practice, and the ways in which communities interpret the meaning of leadership in the Muslim world.

The most basic difference between Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims concerns the question of succession after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. Sunni Muslims generally hold that the Prophet did not explicitly designate a political and religious successor and that the Muslim community was therefore permitted to choose a leader through consultation and consensus. From this perspective, Abu Bakr, a close companion of the Prophet and his father-in-law, was the first rightful caliph. This was followed by Umar, Uthman, and Ali, who are known in Sunni tradition as the “Rightly Guided Caliphs.” For Sunnis, leadership is primarily a matter of communal responsibility and political legitimacy. The caliph is expected to uphold Islamic law, protect the community, and serve as a steward of public order, but he is not regarded as divinely appointed or spiritually infallible.

Shi‘a Muslims, by contrast, believe that the Prophet Muhammad designated Ali ibn Abi Talib, his cousin and son-in-law, as his successor. The word “Shi‘a” derives from the Arabic term shi‘at Ali, meaning “the party of Ali.” Shi‘a Muslims hold that leadership of the Muslim community was not left to human choice but was a divinely ordained matter. In this view, Ali was the first Imam, and the Imamate passed through his descendants and through Ali’s wife Fatimah, the Prophet’s daughter. Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

# Pitch Deck: Tabletoply

## 1. Cover Slide

**Tabletoply**  
The Social Network for Board Game Society

**Tagline:**  
Find players, discover games, and build your tabletop community.

**One-Line Summary:**  
Tabletoply is a social network built around board games, helping players organize meetups, track collections, and connect with nearby gaming communities.

---

## 2. Problem

Board gamers are scattered across fragmented platforms.

Today, players use:

- Facebook groups for local meetups
- BoardGameGeek for reviews and collections
- Discord for event coordination
- Reddit for discussions
- Meetup or Eventbrite for scheduled play nights
- Private chats to coordinate games

**The result:**

- Hard to find reliable local players
- Event discovery is inconsistent
- Game recommendations are generic
- Communities are siloed
- New players struggle to join the hobby
- Experienced players lack a home for their tabletop identity

There is no dedicated social network designed around the full board game experience.

---

## 3. Solution

**Tabletoply is a social network for board gamers.**

It combines:

- Player profiles
- Game collections
- Local meetup discovery
- Event scheduling
- Group chat
- Game recommendation engine
- Community forums
- Marketplace for trading or selling games
- Reputation system for trusted players

**Core value proposition:**  
Everything a board gamer needs to find games, meet people, and manage their tabletop life in one place.

---

## 4. Market Opportunity

The board game market is growing rapidly.

**Market drivers:**

- Board games have moved beyond family entertainment into a mainstream hobby
- Tabletop gaming communities are expanding globally
- Cafés, conventions, and local gaming groups are increasing
- Players want social, in-person experiences
- Digital tools are still fragmented

**TAM:**  
Global board game market valued in the tens of billions of dollars.

**SAM:**  
Millions of active hobby board gamers, including casual players, collectors, event organizers, and content creators.

**SOM:**  
Early focus on urban board gaming communities, local meetups, game cafés, and convention attendees.

---

## 5. Product

### User Profile

Each player has a profile featuring:

- Favorite games
- Collection
- Play style
- Location
- Availability
- Experience level
- Reputation score

### Game Database

Users can:

- Search games
- Track owned games
- Build wishlists
- Rate and review games
- Save game preferences

### Local Community

Tabletoply connects players with:

- Nearby meetups
- Game cafés
- Local groups
- Casual play sessions
- Competitive events
- Convention meetups

### Events

Users can:

- Create events
- RSVP to games
- Invite friends
- Set player limits
- Track attendance
- Receive reminders

### Social Feed

A board game-specific social feed allows users to:

- Post game sessions
- Share photos
- Write short reviews
- Ask questions
- Join discussions
- Follow creators and communities

---

## 6. Product Features

### Core Features

1. **Player Matching**  
   Match players by location, availability, game preferences, and experience level.

2. **Event Discovery**  
   Find board game meetups, café nights, conventions, and private sessions.

3. **Game Collection Tracker**  
   Keep track of owned, borrowed, and wanted games.

4. **Community Groups**  
   Create private or public groups for friends, clubs, cities, or game genres.

5. **Smart Recommendations**  
   Suggest games and events based on user preferences and social activity.

6. **Trusted Player Reputation**  
   Build trust through event attendance, reviews, and community feedback.

i was folding a sandwich into a tiny triangle when the floor admitted it had a secret.
the secret was soft and round and smelled like a library sneezing.
my spoon pointed at a map, but the map was wearing boots.
the boots walked in a circle and said, "hi, we are not flat, we are cheeky."
i told the sandwich to keep its opinion inside its bread.
the sandwich said bread has no opinion, only crumbs.
then the horizon did a slow backflip over the parking lot.
it looked like a turtle made of weather, and i felt very suspicious of turtles.
i asked a pigeon for legal advice, but the pigeon was busy being a cloud.
the cloud-pigeon dropped a feather shaped like a tiny planet.
when i touched it, my fingers learned a new language called gravity.
gravity said, "hello, you are not stuck to a board, you are loved by a ball."
i replied that balls are fun but also suspicious at parties.
the earth laughed in a way that made my socks slide toward the south.
i had always believed the world was a very patient pancake.
apparently it was more like a moody orange with oceans.
this made me feel like a fruit inspector.
i climbed a hill to test the theory, but the hill was already curved and smug.
ships went down there like polite submarines with hats.
stars leaned in and whispered that they had been watching me be confused for years.
the moon made a face and said, "flat is a myth invented by napkins."
i tried to argue with the moon, but the moon had better grammar.
i sat on the round earth and felt strangely hugged.
it was not a flat hug, it was a spherical hug with weather in it.
i told my shoes, and my shoes started walking in circles to celebrate.
the sandwich got jealous and declared itself a tiny globe.
i ate it, because truth is sometimes delicious and slightly salty.
the earth said nothing after that, but its curve hummed a lullaby.
i now believe the world is not flat, and also i believe in polite hats.
this is my weird proof, and it fits in my pocket like a round secret.

🚀 What if you could test the impossible before it ever exists?

That is the question we started asking when we founded SimForge Labs, a startup building a cloud platform for realistic physics simulation. We wanted to give engineers, designers, researchers, students, and creators a place where they could run complex simulations without owning a supercomputer, hiring a specialist team, or waiting weeks for results. We wanted physics simulation to feel as simple as opening a browser tab.

For too long, realistic simulation has been locked behind expensive licenses, heavy desktop software, and steep learning curves. A small robotics team may not be able to afford the tools needed to test a new gripper. A startup may not be able to crash-test hundreds of drone designs in the real world. A game studio may spend months trying to make debris behave naturally. A university class may only have one shared workstation. We think that is backwards. If physics is universal, the tools to explore it should be accessible.

Our platform lets users build, run, and share simulations from any device. You can upload a model, define materials, set forces, and watch the results unfold with realistic motion, collision, deformation, and fluid behavior. You can tweak parameters and compare outcomes side by side. You can save experiments, revisit old runs, and explain your results with visual timelines. Whether you are designing a bridge, simulating a fall, testing a prosthetic joint, or creating a realistic explosion effect in a game, the goal is the same: make the simulation feel believable, useful, and fast.

Why does that matter? Because the real world is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous. Building physical prototypes costs money. Crashing them costs more. Some tests are difficult to repeat fairly. Some are too hazardous to perform often. A platform for realistic physics simulation helps teams ask better questions earlier. It helps them fail safely, iterate quickly, and make decisions with confidence. It turns “what if” into “let’s test it now.”

فاطمہ: سچ؟ اس کتاب کا موضوع کیا ہے؟

فاطمہ: کیا کتاب میں کوئی کمی محسوس ہوئی؟

علی: ہاں، کچھ جگہوں پر مشورے بہت عام لگتے ہیں۔ بچوں کی مختلف ضرورتوں کے لیے مزید تفصیلی مثالیں، خاص طور پر نوجوانوں اور ان بچوں کے لیے جنہیں پڑھائی میں دشواری ہوتی ہے، ضروری تھیں۔

## *A Short Tour of the Dutch Language*

Dutch is the official language of the Netherlands and Suriname, and it is also spoken in Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten. With around 25 million speakers, it is not one of the world’s most widely spoken languages, but it has a rich history and some surprisingly interesting features.

One of the first things people notice about Dutch is that it sits between English and German. It has German-like grammar and vocabulary, but many words feel closer to English. For example, the English word “water” is also “water” in Dutch. The word “house” becomes “huis,” and “book” becomes “boek.” This makes Dutch feel familiar to English speakers while still having its own distinct character.

Dutch also has a fun relationship with compound words. Like German, Dutch can combine smaller words into longer ones. A “treinwagon” is a train wagon, and “ijsbeer” literally means “ice bear,” which is the word for “polar bear.” Some compounds are practical, while others are delightfully descriptive.

## *Why Dutch Sounds Different Than You Expect*

Another interesting fact is that Dutch has sounds that can surprise English speakers. The “g” sound is often pronounced with a throaty “ch”-like sound, especially in the Netherlands. In Belgium, Dutch speakers may use a softer “g,” which can make spoken Dutch sound quite different depending on the region.

Dutch also uses the letter combination “ij,” which is treated as a single unit in some contexts. It is not simply an “i” followed by a “j.” This can be confusing for learners, especially because “ij” and “ei” sound very similar but can change the meaning of a word completely.

Dutch is a language full of small surprises: familiar words, tricky pronunciation, and playful compound words. Whether you are learning it, comparing it to English, or simply curious about linguistics, Dutch shows how closely related languages can still develop their own personality.

Unlike parks shaped primarily for recreation, wilderness areas protect ecological processes that have developed over thousands of years. Rivers flow without dams, forests grow and burn in natural cycles, and animals move across landscapes that remain largely untouched by human development. *Wilderness is not merely empty land; it is a living archive of ecological memory.*

Preserving wilderness also requires addressing the knot of modern pressure: expanding cities, resource extraction, tourism, and climate change. These forces can tighten around fragile ecosystems like a knot, making protection more urgent. Governments, Indigenous communities, scientists, and ordinary citizens must work together to create protected corridors, enforce conservation laws, and support sustainable economies. *Protecting wilderness is not an act of retreat from progress, but a commitment to a wiser form of progress.*

In the end, wilderness preservation is both a practical and moral responsibility. It asks societies to limit consumption, respect nonhuman life, and leave room for nature to continue its own story. If we learn to untie the knot of short-term greed and long-term neglect, we can preserve wild lands not as relics, but as enduring sources of life, beauty, and resilience.

Für die USA zeigen gängige Auswertungen wie OpenSecrets in den letzten Jahren ein ähnliches Bild: Amazon liegt regelmäßig vorn, Microsoft und Alphabet/Google folgen dicht, während Apple und Meta/Facebook vergleichsweise niedrigere Ausgaben melden.

Zusammenfassung:

- **Amazon**: gehört zu den größten Lobbyingspendern. Die jährlichen Ausgaben lagen zuletzt oft im oberen einstelligen bis niedrigen zweistelligen Millionenbereich.
- **Google / Alphabet**: ebenfalls unter den Top-Lobbyisten, mit jährlichen Ausgaben im hohen einstelligen bis niedrigen zweistelligen Millionenbereich.
- **Microsoft**: sehr aktiver Lobbyist, meist in ähnlicher Größenordnung wie Google, oft im hohen einstelligen bis niedrigen zweistelligen Millionenbereich.
- **Apple**: deutlich geringere gemeldete Lobbying-Ausgaben als Amazon, Microsoft und Google, aber weiterhin im sechsstelligen bis niedrigen Millionenbereich.
- **Facebook / Meta**: ähnlich wie Apple, mit moderateren Ausgaben, meist im sechsstelligen bis niedrigen Millionenbereich.

Insgesamt geben Amazon, Microsoft und Google deutlich mehr für Lobbying aus als Apple und Meta. Meta und Apple konzentrieren sich häufiger auf einzelne Regulierungsthemen wie Datenschutz, App-Stores oder Wettbewerbsrecht, während Amazon, Google und Microsoft breiter in Technologie-, Steuer-, Handels- und Regulierungsthemen vertreten sind.

<<Critique of Cohen Dating App Ad Copy>>

The ad copy is clear and easy to understand, but it is too generic and lacks a strong value proposition.

Strengths:
- The opening line is direct: “Meet your new match!”
- It quickly explains what the app does: matching based on interests and location.
- The call to action is simple: “Download Cohen today.”

Weaknesses:
- “Cohen is a free app that matches you with others based on your interests and location” sounds like many other dating apps and does not differentiate the brand.
- “Find love, friendship, or just someone to swing with” mixes serious and casual messaging in a way that may confuse the target audience. “Swing with” is also ambiguous and could be interpreted as sexually suggestive, which may not fit a new or broad dating app launch.
- The copy lacks emotional appeal or a compelling benefit. It tells users what the app does, but not why they should care or what makes Cohen better than existing apps.
- There is no sense of safety, trust, or community, which are important in dating app marketing.
- “Download Cohen today and start meeting new people!” is a weak CTA. It could be more specific and action-oriented.

Overall, the ad copy needs a clearer brand identity, stronger differentiation, and a more focused tone.

**One-Line Pitch**  
TerritoryMail helps local businesses, freelancers, and service providers send personalized physical letters to people in their territory—even if they don’t know them personally—using compliant, targeted, and automated direct-mail campaigns.

---

## 1. Problem

Many local businesses struggle to reach nearby customers because digital ads have become expensive, crowded, and easy to ignore.

At the same time, traditional direct mail is:

- Complicated to set up  
- Expensive to test  
- Hard to target  
- Difficult to personalize  
- Time-consuming to manage  

Small businesses, real estate agents, contractors, lawyers, coaches, and local service providers often want to reach specific neighborhoods or territories but don’t know who to send letters to or how to do it at scale.

---

## 2. Solution

TerritoryMail is a simple platform that lets users:

1. Define a service area or territory  
2. Select the type of audience they want to reach  
3. Generate or upload a personalized letter  
4. Send physical letters to people in that territory  
5. Track responses through QR codes, promo codes, tracked phone numbers, or landing pages  

The goal is to make cold outreach through physical mail as simple as sending an email campaign.

---

## 3. Why Physical Letters?

Physical letters stand out because:

- They are not filtered into spam  
- They feel more personal and trustworthy  
- They are often read within 24–48 hours  
- They work well for local trust-based services  
- They can be paired with digital follow-up  

For many local businesses, a well-written letter can outperform a cold email or social media ad because it feels intentional rather than automated.

---

TerritoryMail is for:

- Local service businesses  
- Real estate agents  
- Home contractors  
- Insurance agents  
- Financial advisors  
- Attorneys  
- Coaches and consultants  
- Political candidates  
- Nonprofits  
- Local restaurants and retail stores  

These customers often need to reach a specific geographic area, not a global audience.

---

Users draw or select a neighborhood, ZIP code, radius, or custom territory.

- Recently moved residents  
- Family status  
- Local business category

Users choose from proven letter templates or write their own.

The platform can improve the letter using AI suggestions for:

- Tone  
- Clarity  
- Call to action  
- Local relevance  
- Compliance-safe language  

### Personalization
Letters can include:

- Name  
- Street or neighborhood reference  
- Local landmark  
- Offer code  
- Sender signature  
- Business logo  
- QR code for tracking  

### Compliance Layer
TerritoryMail helps users avoid illegal or spammy outreach by:

- Checking for do-not-mail lists where applicable  
- Providing compliant letter language  
- Requiring opt-out mechanisms  
- Storing consent or lawful basis records where needed  

### Tracking and Follow-Up
Each letter can include:

- Unique QR codes  
- Personalized URLs  
- Promo codes  
- Tracked phone numbers  
- Response forms  

Users can follow up with email, SMS, or a second letter.

---

A local roofing company wants to reach homeowners in a 10-mile radius.

Using TerritoryMail, the owner:

1. Draws the territory on a map  
2. Filters for homeowners aged 35–70  
3. Selects a “storm damage inspection” letter template  
4. Adds a 15% inspection discount code  
5. Sends 500 letters  
6. Tracks QR code responses  
7. Follows up with interested leads by phone or email  

Instead of guessing who to contact, the business reaches a focused local audience with a physical letter.

---

### Pay-Per-Letter
Customers pay a per-mail price that includes:

- Printing  
- Postage  
- Letter fulfillment  
- Basic tracking  

Example pricing:

- $0.85 to $1.50 per letter depending on volume and format

<<Sleep Through the Night: A Professional Rap>>

Yo, gather round, clinicians, nurses too,  
We’re breaking down infant sleep, here’s what to do.  
No magic trick, no one-size-fits-all rhyme,  
We need plans that work in real life, one time.

*Assess the age and health: infants under 4–6 months may still need night feeds; rule out reflux, allergy, growth spurts, or illness.*

Start with the routine, keep it calm and tight,  
Dim the lights, lower voices, set the scene right.  
Feed, bathe, book, cuddle, then bed,  
Predictable patterns help the little one settle instead.

Watch wake windows, don’t let them crash,  
Overtired babies fight sleep in a flash.  
Look for cues: yawning, rubbing eyes, fussing,  
Then start the wind-down, don’t keep them bustling.

*Build the environment: dark room, white noise, safe crib, firm mattress, back to sleep, no soft bedding or overheating.*

Put baby down when drowsy, not fully out,  
That’s the skill that helps self-soothing grow about.  
If they cry, respond with support, not panic,  
Pause, check, comfort, then try it again—practice.

For older infants, check the day,  
Enough feeds, play, naps, and sleep away.  
Daytime calories matter, don’t skip,  
A hungry baby won’t settle quick.

Sleep associations can make nights rough,  
Rocking, feeding, pacifiers—sometimes that’s enough.  
If parents want change, fade it slow,  
Less help each night, let the baby take control.

Track the logs: bedtime, wakings, feeds,  
Patterns show you where the issue leads.  
Adjust gradually, give it a week,  
Consistency’s the beat that makes sleep speak.

P.P.S Always individualize guidance and refer to pediatric care when needed.

<<Choke on the Potomac>>

I was biting into summer,  
a crisp, hot, golden bite,  
by the Potomac’s silver current,  
under Washington’s light.

I laughed, then the world went quiet,  
my throat shut like a door,  
a piece of chicken caught in the dark,  
and the river kept roaring for more.

Choking, choking,  
on the old Potomac shore,  
no words, no scream,  
just the water and the floor.

Hands up, hands out,  
the crowd turned pale and still,  
the boats kept drifting past me,  
the tide rolling in and out.

Then a stranger stepped beside me,  
said, “Lean down, push, and breathe,”  
like a prayer in a panic,  
like hope I couldn’t believe.

One hard thrust, then a coughing,  
a gasp, then the air came back,  
the river flashed in the sunset,  
and I felt the beat of my heart.

Choking, choking,  
but I’m living, I’m here,  
with chicken on my conscience  
and the Potomac in my ear.

Now every bite is a promise,  
every breath is a song,  
I survived on the Potomac
